title: ESSAY 10: Green Finance and Sustainable Banking in India

blocks.content: (Word Count: ~300 words | Type: Contemporary/Analytical | Level: RBI Grade B / NABARD / SBI PO)

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Green finance integrates environmental, social, and governance (ESG) criteria into financial decision-making and capital allocation.
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) introduced renewable energy projects under Priority Sector Lending (PSL) to enhance institutional credit availability.
SEBI replaced Business Responsibility Reporting (BRR) with the comprehensive Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting (BRSR) framework.
Sovereign Green Bonds (SGBs) allow the Government of India to channel public debt specifically toward low-carbon infrastructure projects.
Sustainable banking incorporates physical and transition climate risks into the credit risk assessment frameworks of commercial banks.

blocks.content: Sustainable banking is not merely a social obligation but a strategic necessity to manage climate risks and build economic resilience in India.

As the world grapples with the existential threat of climate change, the financial sector faces a pivotal question: can capital be mobilised to accelerate the transition to a sustainable economy, and can banks be reoriented from passive bystanders to active agents in addressing the climate crisis? India, as the world's third-largest emitter of greenhouse gases and simultaneously one of the most climate-vulnerable nations, sits at the very centre of this question.

rows: Maximizing profit and traditional financial return on equity
Triple Bottom Line: People, Planet, and Profit
Evaluates financial, market, and operational credit risks
Incorporates ESG parameters and long-term climate transition risks
Agnostic to carbon footprint or environmental degradation
Prioritizes renewable energy, green building, and clean technology

blocks.content: Green finance — the allocation of financial resources to projects and activities with positive environmental outcomes — is gaining rapid momentum in India. The Government of India issued its inaugural Sovereign Green Bonds in January 2023, raising Rs. 16,000 crore for green infrastructure projects including renewable energy, clean transportation, and sustainable water management. India's green bond market, while still nascent compared to those of China and the European Union, is growing at over 40% annually, driven by corporate issuances from renewable energy companies and infrastructure developers. The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) has mandated detailed ESG (Environmental, Social, and Governance) disclosures from the top 1,000 listed companies, creating a transparency framework that enables investors to make climate-informed decisions.

The Reserve Bank of India has begun integrating climate risk into the supervisory framework. RBI's Discussion Paper on Climate Risk and Sustainable Finance (2022) identified physical risks (damage from extreme weather events) and transition risks (financial impact of shifting to a low-carbon economy) as material threats to bank balance sheets. Banks are being encouraged to develop climate stress testing frameworks and to incorporate environmental factors into their credit appraisal processes — a fundamental shift in how risk is conceived.

items: RBI's Priority Sector Lending guidelines cover solar, wind, and biomass energy projects up to a borrowing limit of ₹30 crore per borrower.
SEBI's BRSR framework is mandatory for the top 1,000 listed entities by market capitalization in India.
Distinction between 'Greenwashing' (misleading environmental claims) and authentic green financial products is frequently tested in UPSC and RBI Grade B examinations.

blocks.content: The challenge lies in the vast scale of financing required. India needs an estimated $2.5 trillion to meet its clean energy transition targets by 2030. Blended finance models — combining commercial bank lending, development finance, and concessional public funding — must be deployed creatively. As RBI, NABARD, and IREDA (Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency) build India's green finance architecture, the banking sector's commitment to sustainability will increasingly define its licence to operate in a carbon-constrained world.

Examiner's Tip: Green Finance is an emerging but important topic for RBI Grade B and NABARD exams. Mention Sovereign Green Bonds, SEBI ESG disclosures, RBI's climate risk discussion paper, and blended finance. This shows cutting-edge awareness.
